summary: A Network Host Status report from Ellen Westheimer of BBN covering March 27 to April 7, 1972. During this time the Ames PDP-10 acting as front end to the Illiac became a server, though not for general use for months. A terminal IMP was installed at the University of Southern California on March 29. It updates RFC 326.

plainLanguage.summary: This report gives host status predictions and connection-test results for late March and early April 1972. It notes two changes in the network: an Ames host became a server, and USC received a Terminal IMP.

subtitle: A Network Host Status report covering March 27 to April 7, 1972.

tldr.problem: Network users needed a current account of which hosts could provide services and which were available only as users.
tldr.mechanism: BBN's report lists host status predictions and records connection-test results on selected dates.
tldr.outcome: An Ames PDP-10 acting as an Illiac front-end became a server, and a Terminal IMP was installed at USC. RFC 330 obsoletes RFC 326 and was updated by RFC 332.

today: RFC 330 is listed as Unknown. It obsoletes RFC 326 and was updated by RFC 332.

sections.title: Changes During the Period
sections.content:
This RFC reports on most Network Hosts from March 27 to April 7. During that time, the PDP-10 at Ames that acted as a front-end to the Illiac, Network Address 15, became a server. The report says it would not be available for general use for several months.

A Terminal IMP was installed at the University of Southern California, Network Address 23, on March 29. The RFC header says it updates RFC 326 and obsoletes none.
sections.plainLanguage: The report records two changes: an Ames computer began serving the network, and USC received a Terminal IMP. The Ames host was not yet ready for general use.

sections.title: Hosts Excluded from Testing
sections.content:
Some hosts are excluded because they are not expected to function regularly as servers for at least two weeks. Others are intended to be users only. The latter group includes Terminal IMPs, the Network Control Center computer used to gather statistics, and several site computers named in the report.

The BBN Terminal IMP at Network Address 158 is a prototype. It is frequently disconnected while its programs are refined and debugged. A star in the status tables identifies hosts not included in daily testing.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers are left out of the tests because they are not ready to serve other sites or are intended only to use network services.

sections.title: Test Tables and Status Codes
sections.content:
The tables list host status predictions and test results for ten dates between March 27 and April 7. Codes identify open, dead, half-open, timed-out and refused connections. A timeout means the host did not complete the Initial Connection Protocol and open a connection within 60 seconds.

A hash mark means the site had advertised that its system might not be available. The UCLA IBM-360/91 offered NETRJS, but the BBN Terminal IMP could not test that service; the report treated an initial connection to its logger as evidence that NETRJS worked.
sections.plainLanguage: Each test gets a short code describing its result. A hash mark means the site had warned that it might be unavailable.

references.text: RFC 326, the earlier host status report obsoleted by this RFC.
